questions.question_text: What is the class centre of the class interval $35 - 44$?

options.why: Calculated the midpoint of 35 and 45 instead of using the given upper limit 44.
Subtracted half the class width from the lower limit instead of finding the midpoint.
Added half the class width to the upper limit instead of averaging endpoints.

questions.question_text:
A grouped frequency table has frequencies $7, 14, 21, 12, 6$ across five consecutive class intervals.
What is the cumulative frequency of the fourth class interval?

options.why: Calculated the cumulative frequency of the third class interval instead of the fourth.
Reported the frequency of the fourth class interval rather than its cumulative frequency.
Reported the total cumulative frequency of all five classes.

questions.question_text:
In a traffic survey of $50$ vehicles, the class interval $60 - 69\text{ km/h}$ has a frequency of $18$.
What is the relative frequency of this class expressed as a decimal?

options.why: Wrote the frequency with a decimal point instead of dividing by the total of 50.
Divided the frequency by 40 instead of the total sample size of 50.
Multiplied the frequency by 4 instead of dividing by the total sample size.

questions.question_text:
The relative frequencies for four score intervals in a fitness test are shown in the table.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}\text{Score}&20-39&40-59&60-79&80-99\\ \hline \text{Relative frequency}&0.12&0.28&0.35&0.25\end{array}$
What is the estimated probability that a randomly selected participant scored $60$ or more (in the top two classes)?

options.why: Reported the relative frequency of only the $60-79$ class rather than summing both top classes.
Summed the relative frequencies of the first three classes ($0.12 + 0.28 + 0.35$) instead of the top two.
Calculated the probability of scoring in the bottom two classes ($0.12 + 0.28$) instead of the top two.
Counted only the class with class centre 30, omitting higher classes.
Counted classes strictly above 30 (40 and 50) rather than 30 or higher.
Included class centre 20 in the sum (9 + 15 + 8 + 4).
Reported the cumulative frequency at age 60 instead of subtracting the previous cumulative frequency.
Reported the cumulative frequency at age 40 instead of the class frequency.
Added the two cumulative frequencies (34 + 70) instead of finding their difference.

questions.question_text: Why is continuous numerical data (such as student heights) grouped into class intervals for display rather than listed in an ungrouped frequency table?

options.text: Individual continuous measurements rarely repeat exactly, so an ungrouped table would consist of many single entries of frequency $1$.
Grouping continuous data allows exact calculations of the mean and median to be performed.
options.why: Grouped data yields only estimates of summary statistics, not exact values.

options.text: Continuous data can only ever take integer values, which must be grouped into bins.
options.why: Continuous data can take any real value on an interval, not only integers.

options.text: Ungrouped frequency tables cannot be used for datasets containing more than $10$ scores.
options.why: Ungrouped tables can be used for any size dataset where discrete scores repeat.

questions.solution_text:
Continuous data takes on a wide range of values where individual measurements rarely repeat.
Grouping into class intervals summarises patterns and trends that would otherwise be obscured by single-frequency entries.

questions.question_text:
In a grouped dataset of $200$ customer transactions, the relative frequency of the modal class is $0.32$.
If $25$ new customer transactions are recorded, and all $25$ fall into this same modal class, what is the new relative frequency of this class correct to $3$ decimal places?

options.why: Divided 89 by 200 instead of updating the total sample size to 225.
Added 0.125 directly to the relative frequency without recomputing over the new total.
Assumed the relative frequency remains unchanged after adding 25 observations.

questions.question_text:
An ogive displays the test marks of $160$ candidates.
The cumulative frequency reaches $40$ at mark $50$, $100$ at mark $65$, and $144$ at mark $80$.
What percentage of candidates scored between $50$ and $80$ marks?

options.why: Calculated the percentage between 50 and 65 marks (60/160) rather than between 50 and 80.
Calculated the cumulative percentage at 80 marks (144/160) without subtracting the lower mark.
Calculated the percentage below 50 marks (40/160) instead of between 50 and 80.

questions.question_text:
Which of these data sets is represented in the histogram shown below?
The histogram has class intervals 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80 and 80–100, with frequencies 1, 5, 4, 4 and 1 respectively.

options.why: Its values produce different frequencies across the five histogram intervals.
It contains too many values and does not match the displayed bin frequencies.
It has only seven values, so its interval frequencies are too small.

questions.solution_text: Counting option B in the intervals gives 1 value from 0–20, 5 from 20–40, 4 from 40–60, 4 from 60–80 and 1 from 80–100. These match the histogram exactly.
